Jessica the jackrabbit wants to climb down a wall. The wall consists of 2026 horizontal layers stacked vertically. The $n$th layer from the top is partitioned into $2^n - 1$ identical rectangular bricks arranged side by side. Jessica begins in the topmost layer, which contains a single brick. A move consists of Jessica going down one layer to a brick that shares a side with the brick she is currently on.

Determine, with proof, the total number of distinct sequences of moves Jessica can take to reach the 2026th layer.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let the common width of the wall be \(1\). In layer \(n\), there are

\[
m_n=2^n-1
\]

bricks. Number the bricks in layer \(n\) from left to right by \(1,2,\dots,m_n\). The \(i\)-th brick in layer \(n\) occupies the horizontal interval

\[
I_{n,i}=\left[\frac{i-1}{m_n},\frac{i}{m_n}\right].
\]

Since \(m_{n+1}=2m_n+1\), the \(j\)-th brick in layer \(n+1\) occupies

\[
I_{n+1,j}=\left[\frac{j-1}{2m_n+1},\frac{j}{2m_n+1}\right].
\]

Two bricks in consecutive layers share a side exactly when their horizontal intervals overlap in a segment of positive length.

Fix a layer \(n\), and let \(a=m_n\). For the \(i\)-th brick in layer \(n\), its endpoints are

\[
x=\frac{i-1}{a},\qquad y=\frac{i}{a}.
\]

We claim this brick touches exactly the bricks \(2i-1\), \(2i\), and \(2i+1\) in layer \(n+1\).

First,

\[
\frac{2i-2}{2a+1}\le \frac{i-1}{a}\le \frac{2i-1}{2a+1},
\]

so the left endpoint \(x\) lies in the horizontal span of brick \(2i-1\). Similarly,

\[
\frac{2i}{2a+1}<\frac{i}{a}\le \frac{2i+1}{2a+1},
\]

so the right endpoint \(y\) lies in the horizontal span of brick \(2i+1\). Moreover,

\[
\frac{i-1}{a}<\frac{2i-1}{2a+1}<\frac{2i}{2a+1}<\frac{i}{a},
\]

so the entire brick \(2i\) in layer \(n+1\) lies under brick \(i\) in layer \(n\).

If \(j\le 2i-2\), then brick \(j\) in layer \(n+1\) ends at or before \(x\), so it cannot share a side with brick \(i\). If \(j\ge 2i+2\), then brick \(j\) begins at or after \(y\), so it also cannot share a side with brick \(i\). Hence each brick has exactly three valid downward moves.

Thus every partial sequence ending in layer \(n\) can be extended in exactly \(3\) distinct ways to layer \(n+1\). Starting with \(1\) brick in layer \(1\), the number of sequences reaching layer \(n\) is

\[
3^{n-1}.
\]

For \(n=2026\), the total number of distinct sequences of moves is

\[
\boxed{3^{2025}}.
\]
